past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: Isotopes of an element can be identified by their I. mass number (A) II. charge number (Z) III. neutron number (N)
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number (charge number Z) but different mass numbers (A) due to a different number of neutrons (N). Therefore, they are identified by their mass number (I) and neutron number (III).

past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: Gamma rays have penetration power that is
options: A. less than alpha and beta particles.
B. more than alpha and beta particles.
C. less than alpha, but more than beta particles.
D. more than alpha, but less than beta particles.
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: Gamma rays are high-energy photons with very high penetrating power, significantly greater than that of alpha and beta particles.

past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: If a radioactive element has a half-life of 60 seconds, then the quantity of the isotope after 120 seconds will be
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: Number of half-lives = Total time / half-life = 120 s / 60 s = 2 half-lives. Remaining quantity = $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$ (one-fourth) of the initial quantity.

past_paper_mcqs.stem_text: Nuclear fission reaction can be produced in $_{92}^{238}\text{U}$ by the bombardment of I. fast neutron II. slow neutron III. thermal neutron
past_paper_mcqs.explanation: Uranium-238 ($_{92}^{238}\text{U}$) undergoes nuclear fission only when bombarded with high-energy fast neutrons. In contrast, Uranium-235 undergoes fission with slow/thermal neutrons.

crqs.question: A nuclear fusion reaction is much more difficult to achieve than a nuclear fission reaction. Justify this statement in THREE points.
crqs.answer: 1. Positively charged light nuclei experience strong electrostatic repulsion as they approach each other. 2. Overcoming this Coulomb barrier requires extremely high kinetic energy corresponding to temperatures of millions of kelvins. 3. Containing such high-temperature plasma without melting solid reactor walls is technologically challenging.
crqs.source: AKU-EB SSC-II Model Paper II Q.5

erqs.question: Compare alpha (α), beta (β), and gamma (γ) radiations in terms of their nature, charge, ionising ability, penetrating power, and deflection in electric/magnetic fields.
erqs.answer: Alpha: Helium nucleus (²₄He²⁺), charge +2e, highest ionising power, lowest penetration (stopped by paper). Beta: Fast electron (⁰₋₁e), charge -e, moderate ionisation and penetration (stopped by a few mm of aluminium). Gamma: High-frequency electromagnetic photon, zero charge, lowest ionisation, highest penetration (attenuated by thick lead), undeflected by fields.

numericals.problem:
Suppose a radioactive element has an initial number of atoms ($X$) kept in a nuclear power station.

Calculate the number of radioactive atoms left after $10$ half-lives.
numericals.solution:
**Given Data:**
• Initial number of radioactive atoms ($N_0$) = $X$
• Number of half-lives elapsed ($n$) = $10$

**Formula:**
$$N = N_0 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$

**Substitution & Calculation:**
$$N = X \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{10} = X \times \frac{1}{2^{10}} = \frac{X}{1024}$$

**Answer:**
After $10$ half-lives, $\frac{X}{1024}$ (or $\frac{1}{1024}\text{th}$ of the original number of atoms $X$) will remain undecayed.

numericals.problem: If a radioactive isotope has a half-life of 60 seconds and an initial mass of 80 g, calculate the quantity of the undecayed isotope remaining after 120 seconds.
numericals.formula: N = N₀ × (1/2)^n, where n = t / T_½
numericals.solution: Number of half-lives n = 120 s / 60 s = 2. Remaining mass N = 80 g × (1/2)² = 80 / 4 = 20 g.

numericals.problem: If a radioactive element has a half-life of 60 seconds, then the quantity of the isotope after 120 seconds will be
numericals.solution: Number of half-lives = Total time / half-life = 120 s / 60 s = 2 half-lives. Remaining quantity = $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$ (one-fourth) of the initial quantity.

numericals.problem: The number of electrons in the isotope of uranium $_{92}\text{U}^{238}$ is
numericals.solution: In a neutral atom represented as $_Z\text{X}^A$, the atomic number $Z = 92$ gives both the number of protons in the nucleus and the number of orbital **electrons** ($92$). (Note: $A = 238$ is the mass/nucleon number and $A - Z = 238 - 92 = 146$ is the number of neutrons).
